Newly hatched chicks of Zoe's imperial pigeon emerge from eggs incubated at 38 °C [T = 38 °C], a temperature that supports optimal embryonic development. Upon hatching, the altricial nestlings are entirely dependent on parental care and weigh approximately 22.6 grams [Ww0 = approximately 22.6 grams], a value inferred from the closely related Torresian imperial pigeon. This initial wet weight, modest in absolute terms, represents roughly four percent of the eventual adult mass. The embryonic period itself is relatively short, with the age at hatching being 27 days [ab = 27 days] under those incubation conditions at a temperature of 38 °C [T = 38 °C]. This developmental duration is consistent with the fast early growth patterns observed in other insular columbids, where predation pressure on nests may select for a shortened incubation period. After hatching, the downy chicks remain in the nest for a further period of parental provisioning, during which they undergo rapid feather development and mass gain under the watchful care of both parents.

As the nestling period progresses, the young birds begin to develop flight feathers and approach the critical milestone of fledging. At a body temperature characteristic of active metabolic periods, approximately 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C], the time from birth to fledging is recorded as 26 days from birth [tx = 26 days from birth]. This pace of development is somewhat accelerated for a pigeon of this size, suggesting that nest predation risk or resource availability in its lowland forest habitat may favor a brief nestling dependency. Following nest departure, the fledglings continue to receive occasional parental feedings while they refine their foraging skills. The subsequent period leading to sexual maturation is more protracted. Puberty, defined by the onset of gonadal development, is reached at 79 days after birth [tp = 79 days after birth], again measured under the same thermal regime of 40.5 °C at a temperature of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C]. This relatively early maturation compared to larger congeners may be linked to high adult mortality rates or a favorable resource environment.

When considering the full life history strategy of the species, the reproductive output is remarkably constrained. Females produce only a single egg per clutch [N_R_i = single egg per clutch], and they raise just one clutch each year [F_R_i = one clutch each year]. This low fecundity is typical of many insular and tropical columbids, where stable environmental conditions and intense competition for nesting sites favor investment in offspring quality over quantity. The first successful breeding attempt is not immediate, however. Under the standard thermal conditions of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C], the time since birth at first brood is 2.3 years since birth [tR = 2.3 years since birth], a significant delay that allows young birds to attain full body size and secure a suitable territory. The prolonged juvenile period is likely reinforced by the need to develop the physiological capacity for sustained flight and efficient fruit processing in the canopy.

The overall life span of the species further emphasizes its slow life history. Maximum longevity under field conditions has been estimated at 15.5 years [am = 15.5 years] when measured against the same thermal regime of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C]. This extended duration is comparable to that of other large-bodied fruit pigeons and reflects the low extrinsic mortality rates typical of island ecosystems with few native predators. The combination of late first reproduction, small clutch size, and a long potential reproductive window suggests a bet-hedging strategy where adult survival buffers the population against occasional years of fruit scarcity. In terms of energetic physiology, the basal metabolic rate of adult birds measured under post-absorptive, resting conditions at 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C] is 306.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 306.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour]. This oxygen consumption value is relatively low for a bird of this mass, consistent with the reduced metabolic demands of a frugivorous, sedentary lifestyle in a warm, stable environment.

The maximum adult body mass recorded for females of Zoe's imperial pigeon reaches 568 grams [Wwi = 568 grams], a figure aligning with the range of 575 to 592 grams (575-592 grams) [Wwi = 575-592 grams] reported in the broader literature for adult females of this species. This substantial mass provides the structural capacity for the processing and transport of large quantities of fruit, which forms the bulk of their diet. Interspecific comparisons within the genus Ducula reveal that this body size is intermediate among the so-called imperial pigeons, with larger species occupying more resource-rich forests and smaller species exploiting marginal habitats. The combination of modest metabolic expenditure, extended lifespan, and low reproductive output paints a clear picture of a K-selected species finely tuned to the predictable productivity of its tropical rainforest environment. Future research should investigate how seasonal fluctuations in fruit availability influence the timing of breeding events and whether the observed thermal profile of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C] represents the species' preferred thermoneutral zone.
